title: ISC U2·W4 — Business Continuity, Disaster Recovery & Resilience (CPA Discipline)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — staying in business when systems fail

The Availability criterion ultimately depends on the ability to keep operating through disruption — a server failure, a ransomware attack, a flood, a regional outage. Business continuity and disaster recovery planning is how an organization prepares to survive these events with minimal damage. This final ISC week covers the difference between the two, the analysis that prioritizes recovery, the key objectives (RTO and RPO), the backup and recovery-site strategies, and the testing that turns a plan on paper into genuine resilience for Meridian Building Group.

Business continuity versus disaster recovery

The two terms are related but distinct. Business continuity planning (BCP) is the broad discipline of keeping the whole business operating during and after a disruption — people, facilities, processes, and communications, not just technology. Disaster recovery (DR) is the subset focused on restoring IT systems and data after a disruptive event. DR answers "how do we get the systems back?"; BCP answers the larger "how does the business keep running — and keep serving customers and meeting obligations — while we do?" A complete program needs both.

The business impact analysis

Planning starts with a business impact analysis (BIA), which identifies the organization's critical business processes and the impact of their disruption over time — financial, operational, legal, and reputational. The BIA determines each process's maximum tolerable downtime (MTD) — how long it can be unavailable before the damage becomes unacceptable — and the resources each depends on. By ranking processes from most to least critical, the BIA drives prioritization: recovery effort and investment go first to the processes whose loss would hurt most, rather than treating every system as equally urgent.

RTO and RPO — the two key objectives

Two objectives quantify the recovery requirement. The recovery time objective (RTO) is the target time to restore a system after a disruption — how quickly it must be back. The recovery point objective (RPO) is the maximum acceptable data loss, expressed as a point in time — how much recent data the organization can afford to lose, which drives backup frequency. Example: an RPO of one hour means backups must occur at least hourly so that no more than an hour of data is lost; an RTO of four hours means the recovery solution must restore service within four hours. Tighter objectives cost more, so they are set per process based on the BIA.

Backup strategies

Backups are the foundation of recovery. A full backup copies all data (slow but simple to restore); an incremental backup copies only data changed since the last backup (fast to take, slower to restore); a differential backup copies data changed since the last full backup (a middle ground). The widely cited 3-2-1 rule — three copies of data, on two different media, with one offsite — guards against localized loss. Critically, backups must be stored offsite (or in a separate cloud region) and tested by restoring them: an untested backup is an assumption, not a control.

Recovery sites and redundancy

To meet aggressive RTOs, organizations maintain alternate recovery sites. A hot site is fully equipped and continuously updated, enabling near-immediate failover — fastest and most expensive. A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs data loading and setup — moderate cost and recovery time. A cold site is just space and infrastructure, requiring everything to be installed — cheapest but slowest. Cloud-based DR increasingly replaces physical sites with on-demand recovery capacity. Within systems, redundancy — failover clusters, redundant power and network, and RAID for disks — provides high availability so a single component failure does not cause an outage at all.

Testing the plan

A plan that is never tested will fail when needed. Organizations test BCP/DR at increasing levels of rigor: a tabletop exercise (the team walks through the plan in a meeting), a simulation/walkthrough (executing parts in a test environment), and a full interruption test (actually failing over to the recovery site — the most realistic and most disruptive). Testing reveals gaps — outdated contact lists, backups that will not restore, dependencies no one documented — and keeps the plan current as systems change. Regular testing, not the existence of a binder, is what produces real recoverability.

From recovery to resilience

Modern practice extends beyond recovering after a failure toward resilience — designing systems and processes to withstand and adapt to disruption with minimal interruption in the first place. Resilience combines high availability, redundancy, distributed cloud architectures, and a tested response capability so that disruptions are absorbed rather than survived. For the accountant, the assurance question is whether the organization has analyzed its critical processes (BIA), set and can meet its RTO/RPO, maintains tested backups and recovery capability, and has rehearsed its response — the controls that make the Availability criterion, and the going-concern assumption behind it, credible.

People, communication, and crisis management

Technology recovery is only half of continuity; the human and communication side is the other. A plan designates a crisis-management team and roles, maintains current contact lists and call trees, and defines how the organization communicates with employees, customers, suppliers, and regulators during a disruption. It addresses alternate work arrangements (remote work, alternate facilities) for events — a pandemic, a fire, a building loss — that affect people and places rather than just systems. Plans stay current through assigned ownership and review after every test or significant system change. A technically flawless recovery still fails if no one knows their role or how to reach customers, which is why BCP reaches well beyond the data center.

Risk transfer and the cost of downtime

Finally, continuity planning weighs risk transfer: cyber-insurance and business-interruption insurance shift part of the financial impact of a disruption to an insurer, complementing — not replacing — the recovery controls. The investment in recovery capability is set against the cost of downtime — lost revenue, contractual penalties, and reputational harm per hour of outage — which makes BCP/DR a cost-benefit decision the CFO co-owns rather than a purely technical one.

CMA bridge

If a disaster takes MBG's systems offline mid-project, the BCP/DR plan determines whether the company bills, makes payroll, and keeps jobs moving or grinds to a halt. The RTO/RPO decisions are financial decisions — how much to invest in recovery capability against the cost of downtime — squarely the kind of risk-versus-cost judgment a CFO makes.

Practice and recap

  1. Distinguish BCP (keep the whole business operating) from DR (restore IT systems and data — a subset of BCP).
  2. Use the business impact analysis to identify critical processes and maximum tolerable downtime, driving prioritization.
  3. Set RTO (target restore time) and RPO (max acceptable data loss → backup frequency); apply backup strategies (full/incremental/differential, 3-2-1, offsite, tested).
  4. Choose recovery sites (hot/warm/cold or cloud) and redundancy (failover, RAID) by RTO; test the plan (tabletop → simulation → full interruption) for genuine resilience.

Recap: business continuity keeps the whole organization operating through disruption while disaster recovery restores its IT systems; a business impact analysis ranks critical processes by maximum tolerable downtime, setting each system's recovery time objective (how fast to restore) and recovery point objective (how much data loss is acceptable, driving backup frequency); recovery rests on tested backups (full/incremental/differential, the 3-2-1 rule, offsite), on hot/warm/cold or cloud recovery sites and redundancy chosen to meet the RTO, and on regular testing (tabletop, simulation, full interruption) — all aimed at resilience that absorbs disruption rather than merely surviving it.

questions.q: Disaster recovery (DR) is best described as:
choices: Restoring IT systems and data — a subset of business continuity
questions.explain: DR focuses on restoring IT; BCP is the broader discipline of keeping the whole business operating.

choices: The maximum acceptable amount of data loss
The target time to restore a system
The cost of a hot site
questions.explain: RPO is the acceptable data loss (a point in time), which drives backup frequency; RTO is the restore-time target.

questions.q: An RPO of one hour means backups must occur:
questions.explain: To lose no more than an hour of data, backups must run at least every hour.

questions.q: Which recovery site offers the fastest failover at the highest cost?
questions.explain: A hot site is fully equipped and continuously updated for near-immediate failover.

choices: 3 copies, on 2 media types, with 1 offsite
questions.explain: 3 copies of data, on 2 different media, with at least 1 stored offsite.

questions.q: A business impact analysis primarily determines:
choices: Critical processes and their maximum tolerable downtime
questions.explain: The BIA ranks critical processes and their tolerable downtime to prioritize recovery.

questions.q: The most realistic (and most disruptive) way to test a DR plan is a:
questions.explain: A full interruption test actually fails over to the recovery site — the most realistic validation.
